1:
Where the prophet saw the Lord standing is the first thing disputed, and the answers are not reconcilable. Ellicott places the vision at the shrine of the calf-worship, with the angel of the presence at the Lord's side to receive the order of destruction, and describes the scene vividly, a crowd of eager devotees round the colossal altar of burnt offering and the shattered ornaments hurled down on them. Clarke, taking the passage as a continuation of what precedes, allows either of the two rival sanctuaries. Gill and Wesley both put it at the altar of burnt offering before the temple at Jerusalem, Gill adding that the Lord had removed from between the cherubim, signalling that he was about to depart and would not be appeased by sacrifice, and Wesley that Israel had forsaken this altar and set up others against it, so that the vision may intimate a coming departure from Judah as well. Calvin argues the point at length and refuses the rival sites outright: had the Lord appeared at either, it would have been an indirect approbation of superstition, and no oracle was ever announced from them. Henry stays with the altar but reads the posture, the Lord removed from the mercy-seat to the judgment-seat, standing there to avenge the quarrel of his altar and to forbid sacrifice.

What was struck is disputed on philological grounds. Ellicott reports that the word mistranslated lintel may mean the wreathed capital of the columns, and that on the same reading the word rendered posts becomes the cornice they support; but since no temple building is mentioned, only the altar, he thinks it safer to keep the ordinary senses and follows the reading that takes the term for the ornamented horns of the altar. Calvin calls it the cover above the posts, and reports that the Hebrew doctors derive the name from the apples or pomegranates painted there, though the round form of the entrance might account for it too. Clarke makes it the timber that binds the wall above the door. On whose head is cut, Clarke offers both a literal demolition and a reading that the heads are the chief men, the priests, prophets and princes marked out for destruction; Calvin takes the head for the priests and rulers and argues that the word following means the common people rather than, as usually given, their posterity; Henry turns it into a figure, smite the king who is the lintel that the princes who are the posts may shake.

On the flight that fails, Ellicott would read break through rather than dig, and sets the dark abode of the gathered dead against heaven the abode of light. Gill is careful that neither the place of the damned nor the grave is meant, since no fugitive would choose either, but the deepest caverns and the very centre of the earth. Keil and Delitzsch make the grammatical observation that carries the passage: the cases named were in fact impossible, and are set out as though possible in order to cut off every escape. Clarke compresses it to the deepest caverns and the most inaccessible heights, from the one dragged up and from the other pulled down. Calvin treats the whole as deliberate hyperbole, all the elements opened as hiding-places and none of them serving, and pauses to reject an absurd handling of the parallel psalm as a statement about the unlimited essence of God, when its point is that we are always in his sight. Henry alone draws a distinction inside the image: those the Lord brings to heaven by grace are never brought down, and only those who climb there by presumption are.
3:
The hiding places are treated briefly and the creature at the bottom of the sea at length. Gill notes only that the mountain named is one of the highest in the land, with woods on it and caves in it, and Clarke says the whole series is metaphorical, meant to show the impossibility of escape. On the serpent the voices diverge. Ellicott identifies it as the water-serpent. Wesley makes it the crocodile or the shark. Calvin reports that some take the word not for a serpent at all but for the whale or leviathan, and grants that elsewhere it does carry that sense, before drawing the point he wants: that the Lord is armed in every element and has means in readiness in all of them. On the captivity Gill offers two constructions, the ordinary one of captives driven before their enemies in triumph, and another by which the going is voluntary flight abroad to escape danger, and he names the flight into Egypt as the instance. Calvin knows the same restriction and refuses it; he will not confine the clause to that one foolish flight, but reads it generally, that exile, commonly called a civil death, would not be the end of evils, since the sword was commanded to pursue the exiles too.

The eye set upon them for evil draws the sharpest comment. Clarke puts it as the turning of a providence: the very care that had once worked for their good is now used against them, so that looking up they see nothing but the terrible lightning-like eye of a sin-avenging God. Wesley reduces it to perpetual watching. Calvin hears a deliberate contrast with the promise that Israel's keeper neither slumbers nor sleeps, and warns that hypocrites lay hold of such promises without repentance and turn them into boasting; the eye is on them still, but to accumulate punishment upon punishment. He then generalises against his own hearers, that nearness to God is no shelter, since those he treats as his family are the more closely observed and the more severely punished if found incurable.

The two verses of power are read by Keil and Delitzsch as a deliberate strengthening of the threat, a description of the Lord of heaven and earth who sends judgments with omnipotent power. Gill takes the same ground, that escape is impossible because he who is omniscient is also omnipotent. Wesley presses the ease of it, no great pains needed but a touch of the finger, and the land melting as snow before the sun; Clarke hears in the melting a continued reference to the earthquake already spoken of. Calvin dissents from the usual handling: this is not a general declaration of power but a special threatening, and the rising and sinking like the great river mean an inundation covering the surface, the sinking to be referred not strictly to the land but to the use men make of it, the bitterness being that where the river's overflow enriches its own country, this one leaves no habitation at all. On the stories built in heaven Gill collects the older opinions, the three elements, the orbs set one above another, or heaven and the heaven of heavens; Clarke reads it from ordinary building, cellar, middle story and housetop, and then enlarges it to the systems ranged through illimitable space; Calvin renders the word ascents or stairs and admits the companion word is difficult, insisting only that whatever it means must be something solid on earth answering to the ascents above.
7:
The comparison with the Cushites is taken two ways. Gill presses the likeness of character: they were no more to God than those people, being blackened by sin and idolaters as they were, and so hardened in the habit of sinning that they could no more change their course than that nation could change its skin. He adds a long note out of the classical writers, who called them the blameless and the honest and made them the first to worship the gods and offer sacrifice, that is, in his judgment, the most religious because the most idolatrous. Clarke identifies them by descent and says only that the whole stock was universally despised, and Ellicott turns that into the question, whether Israel was after all better or safer than a people it despised. Calvin explicitly rejects the reading Gill favours as strained: nothing is said here about an unchanged disposition, only that their condition differs in nothing from the common class of men, and that if God takes away what is his own nothing whatever remains to them. Wesley glosses the nation as a wild, thievish and servile one, and states the argument plainly, that they reason amiss from the deliverance out of Egypt, since that benefit aggravates the sin rather than securing them.

The two other migrations are a matter of geography, and the geography is unsettled. Ellicott records that the old Greek, with the Targums and the Syriac after it, read the first place as Cappadocia, probably from a resemblance of form, that one modern compares an Egyptian name and puts the people in the upper country while another puts them in the delta, and that the identification with Crete is nevertheless the most probable. Clarke names Crete flatly and takes the second place for a city of the Medes; Wesley likewise makes it a country of Media, adding that the people were conquered, sent away there, and at last delivered. Calvin knows a proposal that it means Cyrene and passes it by as doubtful, since the argument does not depend on it: the Philistines were redeemed and so were the Syrians, and therefore redemption was never the peculiar mark of the seed of Abraham.

Whose is the sinful kingdom divides them further. Gill takes it of the ten tribes given to idolatry, Ellicott of the kingdom that had revolted from the true centre of worship, Clarke of Israel as peculiarly sinful and therefore to be signally destroyed by the Assyrian, and Keil and Delitzsch treat the verse as the repetition in plain words of what the opening vision had shown symbolically, election proving no deliverance. Calvin dissents on both halves. The restriction to one kingdom he says militates against the design: the words are indefinite, God summoning all kingdoms to his tribunal. The reservation that follows he refuses to read as the customary mitigation at all, taking it instead as irony aimed at the presumption he has been attacking, as though the prophet asked whether God's hands were tied, whether he must spare the doubly guilty while sparing nobody else. Clarke reads the same clause straight, that the race shall not become extinct but be reserved as monuments of justice and finally of mercy.
9:
The sieve is read in two opposite directions, and the split runs through a single word. Clarke takes the shaking as dispersion over the face of the earth so ordered that the good shall not be lost, and the thing that does not fall he renders a little stone, pebble or gravel, so that not one of them, however little or contemptible, is left behind when the time of a general restoration comes. Wesley says the same more briefly, that though tumbled and tossed with great violence the smallest good grain shall not be lost. Calvin takes the verse the other way, and uses it as his proof that the reservation in the previous verse was irony: had pardon been promised, the prophet would have gone on with that subject, whereas he proceeds in the contrary direction, to say that when the whole floor is cleansed nothing will be found to remain on it, the nation having become empty through its iniquities. On the disputed word he goes against Clarke's rendering: they translate it a stone, he says, but the root means to tie, so that it signifies what is bound or collected, and therefore the solid grain. Gill stands apart from the quarrel, hearing in the command only that afflictive and trying dispensations come by God's appointment and are overruled for his glory.

Calvin then meets the objection his own reading raises. If some godly persons were in the nation, did they fall through as refuse? He answers that the prophet speaks of the body of the people and not of individuals, and that the pious were kept gathered in the sieve, though in a hidden way: on the floor the wheat is beaten with the chaff and no difference can be observed, and it is winnowed with the chaff too, yet the wheat remains. He presses further that even the best of them, named as examples of an almost angelic integrity, went into captivity and could not object that they were punished beyond desert. Keil and Delitzsch supply the frame the others do not state, that because the unchangeable One cannot abolish his purpose of salvation, the destruction of the sinful kingdom is followed by the setting up of the genuine kingdom of God, and they render the promise that follows with a fallen hut, its rents walled up and built as in the days of eternity.

On who dies by the sword the voices agree and differ only in emphasis. Gill describes them as notorious, abandoned to their lusts, obstinate and incorrigible, disbelieving the prophets and putting the evil day far from them. Clarke names the boldest and most incredulous and draws the moral flatly, that it is no evidence of a man's safety that he is presumptuously fearless, and that a blessing belongs to him who trembles at God's word. Wesley puts their saying in their own mouths, that the evil is far off and they will die first and be safe in the grave. Calvin makes security itself the chief mark of impiety, a torpor or rather stupor past remedy in men touched by neither fear nor shame, and he construes the second half of their boast as a denial of nearness rather than of the thing threatened: the prophets said the day was at hand, and these answer that there will be no such haste. He adds the observation that hypocrites grant in general that no one escapes the hand of God, and then quietly except themselves from the common class as though secured by a peculiar privilege.
11:
What the fallen tabernacle is, and when it is raised, is answered on three levels. Wesley keeps it literal: the house of David brought back out of captivity and re-established, fallen by the revolt of the ten tribes and breached by that long division. Gill puts the day forward to the gospel age and reports that the ancient Jewish teachers referred the prophecy to the Messiah, one of the names they gave him being taken from this very verse, the son of the fallen, since he was to spring from David's family when it had sunk into a low condition; he adds that some of them seem to understand the tabernacle of the Messiah's own body to be raised, the human nature being called a tabernacle by the writers of the New Testament. Clarke argues the case negatively and at length: the short prosperity between the Assyrian and the Babylonian captivity cannot answer to closing up breaches and building as in the days of old, nor can the victories of the Asmoneans, which bought only a respite and a very imperfect re-establishment; nothing since has answered either, and so the prophecy remains to be fulfilled. Calvin fastens on the figure itself, that a tabernacle does not comport with royal dignity but describes a mean cottage, and observes that the prophet might have named Jesse and deliberately named David instead, because that name was in repute and the oracle about the fruit of his loins commonly known. Henry reads the same meanness as permanent condition rather than interval, the church militant dwelling as in shepherds' tents to feed and in soldiers' tents to fight, and draws the rule that while the world stands God will have a church in it, and if it be fallen down in one place it shall be raised up elsewhere.

The second verse turns on a textual question that Clarke raises and then refuses. He reports a rendering by which the residue of men seek the Lord rather than possess the remnant of the neighbouring nation, resting on a one-letter difference and supported by the Arabic, some copies of the Syriac and the citation in the book of Acts, together with a Greek manuscript that adds the words that they may seek me. He then notes that not one of the manuscripts collated by the two great collators, nor any of his own, countenances any of these alterations, and concludes that the conjectural emendations must be dismissed and the Hebrew text taken as it stands, the New Testament use being sufficient warrant for the sense without agreement in the words. Gill reads the possession as conversion, the remnant according to the election of grace in nations that had been the greatest enemies, and records that the Targum understands the peoples of the house of Israel itself while other Jewish commentators would invert the clauses. Wesley keeps both senses at once, a literal possession of the land and of some of the people as servants, and a prophecy of the Messiah's kingdom and the bringing in of the Gentiles. Henry takes the enlargement as the accession of whole countries, strangers and enemies becoming willing subjects, and Keil and Delitzsch mark the structure, the outward extension of the kingdom here and its inward glorification in what follows.
13:
The overtaking of the reaper by the ploughman is explained naturally by one voice and figuratively by the rest. Clarke keeps the seasons in their due and natural order and makes the crops so copious that the labours of gathering, treading and sowing press on one another's heels; he supports it from travellers, who report a vintage in those countries running from the middle of September to the middle of November while sowing begins at the close of October, so that the operations genuinely overlap. He concludes even so that what is predicted is fertility, abundance and regularity, and that these are poetical images of happy times. Ellicott says only that the harvest follows the ploughing so rapidly, and that these closing verses foreshadow the glories of the restored kingdom, in which he sees the germ of the later prophecies of the Messiah. Calvin makes the metaphor explicit and defends it: the prophets accommodated their manner of speaking to the notions of an ancient people and spoke to them as to children, borrowing here from a blessing in the law where the vintage meets the harvest, and the mountains running with new wine is frank hyperbole, since we know it never happened. Keil and Delitzsch mark the order of the promises, the richest blessing first of the land, then of the nation, and last the eternal duration of the kingdom.

The objection that none of it came to pass is met by two incompatible answers. Wesley grants the fact and saves the promise by a condition: it never was so because the sins of the returned captives prevented these blessings, which are given under a tacit condition. Calvin grants the same fact and answers instead by transposition. Only a small number returned; so far from ruling the neighbouring nations they became tributary to them, and their borders were narrow even when they threw off the yoke; the promise is therefore seen fulfilled when we come to Christ, since the kingdom was then propagated from the rising to the setting of the sun, and in that sense the Jews reigned. The abundance of corn and wine he explains by the spiritual nature of that kingdom, and he answers the further objection that the prophet is not speaking allegorically by observing that Scripture everywhere paints a happy state by setting the conveniences of the present life before our eyes.

On the planting the voices divide again between a past and a future fulfilment. Gill denies that the return from Babylon can be meant, since those restored were afterwards dispossessed by the Romans and scattered a second time, and takes the captivity to be that of Judah and Israel together, still unended, and the deliverance to be from the bondage of sin and law as well as from exile. Clarke states the same negative more sharply and turns it into a proof: the prophecy has certainly never yet been fulfilled, they were pulled up by one captivity and then another, replanted and pulled up again by the Roman conquest, and never planted since; and because the word of God cannot fail, it therefore will and must be fulfilled. He rests the certainty on the closing formula, that he can do it because he is Jehovah and will do it because he is thy God. Clarke also notices the reversal of an earlier threat, that they should plant vineyards and not drink the wine of them: before their restoration they labour for others, afterwards for themselves. Calvin takes the figure of planting for the settled dwelling itself, since we are flitting beings tossed like chaff unless God locates us, and adds that the gift will hold because God does not regard what the dwellers deserve.
